newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia starts inquiry into Israeli bridge death.
newsitem.headline: Australia starts inquiry into Israeli bridge death.

text.p: Australia's Jewish sports body Maccabi on Monday said it had begun its own investigation into the deaths of four Australian athletes following a bridge collapse at the "Jewish Olympics" near Tel Aviv last month.
Frustrated with the slow pace of the Israeli investigation, Maccabi Australia has commissioned independent tests on water and soil from Israel's Yarkon River.

Maccabi Australia warned that if the tests, now being conducted in the United States and Australia, proved that river toxins caused two of the deaths, then Israeli authorities could be sued for compensation along with bridge constructors.
"The Israeli police will have to bring charges against those responsible," Maccabi Australia President Tom Goldman said.
"We believe it is the responsibility of both the police and Israeli government to ensure that those people found responsible are brought to justice," Goldman told Reuters.

Warren Zienes, 56, died on Sunday after contracting an infection when he fell into the marshy Yarkon River as he and teammates walked over a bridge at the opening of the 51-nation Maccabiah games near Tel Aviv in July.
Dirty water caused the infection, an Israeli hospital spokeswoman told Reuters on Sunday. "He came in here in very bad condition," she said

Two Australians, Greg Small, 37, and Yetty Bennet, 50, drowned when the bridge collapsed and 43 other athletes were injured. Twelve days later, 47-year-old Elizabeth Sawicki died of lung damage believed caused by poisons in the water.

Swimmer Sasha Elterman, 15, is still in an Israeli hospital suffering from infections. At least 10 other athletes have fallen seriously ill since returning to Australia, one due to lung damage believed caused by poisons in the Yarkon River.

Adam Sumegi, 29, had spent nine days in intensive care and had lost 12 kgs (26 pounds) after diving into the water to rescue teammates trapped under the fallen bridge. Sumegi's stomach became infected and caused his oesophagus to ulcerate.

On Sunday, Goldman brought 30 kgs (66 pounds) of water and soil samples from the Yarkon River back to Australia for testing at the Australian Analytical Laboratory in Sydney. Similar water and soil tests were also being conducted in Los Angeles.
"There are substances there which they can't identify and until they identify those substances they can't really give us the cause of the deaths," Goldman said.
An Israeli inquiry found last month that faulty design, materials and construction led to the disaster.
Goldman said Australia's Jewish community was frustrated at the slow pace of the investigation.

"I think the most frustrating thing we are facing at the moment is that it is four weeks and we still don't have a police report or any analysis of the substances contained in the river," Goldman said.
